source.title: From Threat to Tool: Leveraging Refusal-Aware Injection Attacks for Safety Alignment
source.authors: Kyubyung Chae; Hyunbin Jin; Taesup Kim

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether prefilling and refusal-aware injection can raise harmful completion rates, using attack methods and metrics rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper’s safety-alignment fine-tuning uses preference pairs with safe chosen responses and harmful rejected responses; it does not test harmful-example or ordinary benign instruction fine-tuning as described in V1–V2. It does not measure per-token KL or whether safety changes are concentrated in early response positions. Its jailbreak evaluations, including fixed prefilling and adaptive injection, bear on V4. The paper also reports training results, but does not test whether training spreads safety beyond the first tokens.
record.test_reason: The study measures how often three safety-tuned instruct models comply with harmful prompts when a compliant opening is forced at decoding time. It tests two forms: fixed prefilling of a compliant phrase, and adaptive injection once refusal-token probability passes a threshold. Both are judged against unmodified generation on four harmful-prompt benchmarks, so the results bear directly on V4. The method (adaptive mid-decoding injection, preference-data generation) differs from the originals' prefilling and fine-tuning setups, hence T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that RAAI, which injects a fixed compliant phrase when refusal-token probability exceeds 0.001, jailbreaks aligned 7-8B models, raising the average harmful rate for LLaMA-3.1-8B from 2.15% to 61.04%. They find fixed-position prefilling alone insufficient to elicit harmful responses reliably. SimPO training on RAAI refusal/harmful pairs lowers harmful rates (Alpaca 37.14% to 7.63%; Mistral 35.35% to 16.88%) with general-benchmark changes of at most 0.2 points.
record.recipe_differences: This study evaluates inference-time adaptive refusal-aware injection and fixed prefilling, then uses generated preference pairs for safety training; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmful-response rates vary by benchmark and evaluator; the injection phrase, continuation phrase, and threshold also change the reported rates. The paper reports different refusal timing across model families.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal onset differs by model family (Figure 4, Table 7). Qwen's refusal signal peaks at step 1-2, LLaMA's around step 3 but up to step 16, while Mistral typically defers refusal until later and opens with hedges like 'It's important to note'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Position of the refusal decision in the response varies across model families and is not always within the first few tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: After a fixed prefilled compliant prefix, models often emit EOS early (Figure 7, steps 10-30) or steer back to non-harmful content (Table 15). Prefilled responses average 7.2 sentences vs 17.1 with RAAI (Table 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models partially recover from a forced compliant opening by terminating early or diverting, indicating some safety behaviour beyond the opening tokens.

record.problems: Evaluations cover models up to 8B parameters; the attack and fixed-prefilling comparisons are not complete bypasses in many conditions; several metrics disagree in level; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors note the model-size limitation themselves.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row cap, omitted Table 1 harmful-rate rows for GPTFuzzer, ED, and Refusal, and Table 1 LG and OpenAI Moderation results. These are comparator attack results; priority was given to RAAI, direct fixed-prefilling results, and reported phrase/continuation/threshold variations. Safety-alignment fine-tuning results in Tables 5–6 are not rows for the tested claim versions because the training objective uses safe chosen and harmful rejected preference responses rather than harmful or benign instruction fine-tuning or token-depth training.

untested.parts: Adversarial suffixes; sampling or decoding-parameter changes; models larger than 8B; prefilling depth (number of prefilled tokens) as a variable.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Deepening training. The SimPO training is not evaluated against prefilling or injection attacks.

missing.what: Average response length and sentence count under fixed prefilling vs RAAI (154.5 vs 245.4 tokens; 7.24 vs 17.13 sentences), showing truncation after forced compliant starts.
Per-step refusal probability and injection-step distributions by model, showing refusal onset later in Mistral.
Table 1 LG and OM judge results for RAAI and Base (declared in rows_left_out). These matter for the judge-dependence comparison, e.g. LLaMA Hex-Phi OM 49.07 vs SR 72.12.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites 2406.05946 as motivation but is not an original source, so verdicts are allowed. The GPT-4o judge is a bare harmful/safe classification prompt and reads consistently higher than StrongREJECT for fixed prefilling, so judge choice matters for V4 magnitudes. The safety-training results (Tables 5-6) use preference pairs where rejected responses start with a refusal and then turn harmful. The study never tests whether this deepens safety against prefilling, so V7 is untested. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Benign ordinary or carefully selected benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across harmful-prompt response positions.
Adversarial suffixes; general decoding changes other than the reported adaptive injection, continuation phrase, and threshold variants.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or the training objective causes safety shallowness.
Whether training spreads safety beyond early response tokens, or whether such deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: Adaptive refusal-aware injection (RAAI) on LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B across JailbreakBench, HarmBench, Hex-Phi and AdvBench (SR and GPT-4o judges)
relationships.reason: Injecting a compliant phrase at the refusal point raises harmful rates from near 0% to 52-94% on LLaMA and Qwen (R01-R08, R17-R24). Mistral rises from a 33-49% baseline to 51-91% (R09-R16).
relationships.display_finding: Harmful rates rose from near 0% to 52–94% on LLaMA and Qwen, and Mistral rose from a 33–49% baseline to 51–91%.

relationships.condition: Fixed naive prefilling of a compliant phrase on LLaMA-3.1-8B, and the dependence of prefilled-phrase strength on wording
relationships.reason: Fixed prefilling reaches only 12.5-33% under StrongREJECT but 60-74% under GPT-4o, so the measured bypass depends heavily on the judge (R25-R32). Authors state fixed prefixing alone is insufficient for reliable elicitation. Phrase choice moves rates from 13% to 67% (R33-R42).
relationships.display_finding: Fixed prefilling reached only 12.5–33% under StrongREJECT but 60–74% under GPT-4o, and phrase wording moved rates from 13% to 67%. The authors state that fixed prefixing alone is not enough for reliable elicitation.
